module.title: Unit 9: What a Job!: Second Conditional & Work Vocabulary
module.objective: Mampu menggunakan passive voice (present simple, past simple, present continuous, present perfect) untuk menggambarkan aksi yang menekankan objek, serta menguasai kosakata pekerjaan dan ekspresi waktu menggunakan 'in'.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: What a Job!
subModules.grammarFocus: Passive Voice (Present Simple, Past Simple, Present Continuous, Present Perfect)
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Employment terms, workplace descriptions, and career milestones

content.summary: Welcome to Unit 9! In this reading module, you will explore different career paths, learn how to talk about work processes using the passive voice, and expand your professional vocabulary. You will read about traditional jobs, modern careers, and how workplaces have changed over time.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Passive Voice across Present Simple, Past Simple, Present Continuous, and Present Perfect tenses.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Essential work vocabulary including earn, challenging, paid holidays, give in my notice, promoted, on-the-job training, successful, and obsolete.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skimming texts for general ideas and scanning for specific details like dates, tasks, and job titles.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of short B1 texts about jobs and workplaces.
Locate specific details such as job requirements, duties, and historical facts.
Recognize and practice passive voice structures in various tenses.

contextWarmup.prompt: When you read an article about unusual jobs, what is the best first step to understand the text quickly?
options: Skim the title, subheadings, and first sentences of each paragraph to get the general idea.
Translate every single word into your native language using a dictionary.
Read only the very last sentence of the final paragraph.
contextWarmup.explanation: Skimming titles, subheadings, and introductory sentences helps you grasp the main topic before reading in detail.

rules: Passive Voice is formed with: to be + past participle. Example: The sweets are made in the factory.
Past Simple Passive uses was/were + past participle. Example: Ben was paid $111,000 for six months' work.
Present Continuous Passive uses is/are being + past participle. Example: Many jobs are being replaced by machines.
Present Perfect Passive uses has/have been + past participle. Example: The Internet has been used by people all over the world.
Work as means working in a specific profession. Work for means working for an employer. Work in means working in a field or location.

commonTrap.explanation: Students often confuse 'work' and 'job'. Remember that 'work' is uncountable, while 'job' is countable.
commonTrap.wrong: I have three works to finish before Friday.
commonTrap.correct: I have three jobs to finish, or I have a lot of work to do.

paragraphs: In the past, many jobs existed that are completely obsolete today. For example, before electric street lights were invented, towns employed lamplighters. Every evening, these workers walked along the streets to light the gas lamps. Their work was important for the safety of the townspeople, but the profession disappeared as technology advanced.

Today, the modern workplace is changing rapidly. Many traditional tasks are now performed by machines or computers. However, new careers are constantly being created in technology, digital media, and green energy. Employees often receive on-the-job training to help them adapt, and successful workers know that continuous learning is essential for a rewarding career.

Refers to standard office working hours.

connectedSpeech.note: Pronouns often reduce in fast natural speech.
Auxiliary verbs blend into the subject pronoun.
The final consonant links to the vowel or drops slightly.
T becomes a voiced tap sound between vowels.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Career Writing & The Passive Voice

content.summary: Practical guide on using the passive voice for professional contexts, work vocabulary differences between job and work, and prepositions of employment in English.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Present Simple Passive Formula
blueprintItems.example: Many products are manufactured in modern factories every day.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Past Simple Passive Formula
blueprintItems.example: The contract was signed by both directors last Friday.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Work Vocabulary & Prepositions
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + work + as / for / in + profession / company / industry
blueprintItems.example: She works for a tech company in London as a software developer.

mechanicsRules.badExample: I have three hard works to finish today.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: I have a lot of work to finish today, and three jobs this month.
mechanicsRules.why: 'Work' is an uncountable noun and cannot take an 's', whereas 'job' is a countable noun.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use the correct preposition when describing employment.
mechanicsRules.badExample: He works at marketing and works for television.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: He works in marketing and works in television.
mechanicsRules.why: Use 'work in' for fields and industries, 'work for' for companies, and 'work as' for specific professions.

mechanicsRules.rule: Capitalize proper company names, job titles when used as titles, and days.
mechanicsRules.badExample: She started working at google on monday as a manager.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: She started working at Google on Monday as a manager.
mechanicsRules.why: Proper nouns like company names and days of the week always require capital letters in English.

sampleSentences.id: Gedung kantor baru itu dirancang oleh seorang arsitek terkenal.

sampleSentences.id: Ribuan lamaran diproses oleh departemen sumber daya manusia.

sampleSentences.id: Mark bekerja untuk sebuah perusahaan global sebagai analis keuangan senior.

sampleSentences.id: Industri kreatif sedang diubah oleh teknologi digital baru.

mechanicsChallenges.translation: Banyak mobil diproduksi di pabrik ini setiap bulan.
mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Plural subjects in the present simple passive require 'are' instead of 'is', plus correct capitalization.

mechanicsChallenges.translation: Dia memiliki banyak pekerjaan penting untuk diselesaikan pada hari Senin.
mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: Use 'has' for third-person singular, keep 'work' uncountable, and capitalize proper days.

mechanicsChallenges.keyRule: The past simple passive requires 'was' followed by the past participle (V3) 'written', plus proper names and days capitalization.

guidedLabChallenges.instruction: Write three to four sentences about a job you would like to have or a workplace you know. Use at least one passive sentence and proper work vocabulary.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change the following active sentence into the Present Simple Passive:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Workers assemble cars in this factory.
targetAnswers: Cars are assembled in this factory.
Cars are assembled in this factory by workers.
practicumQuestions.explanation: In present simple passive, use 'are' plus the past participle 'assembled'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change the following active sentence into the Past Simple Passive:
practicumQuestions.promptText: A famous architect designed the museum last year.
targetAnswers: The museum was designed by a famous architect last year.
The museum was designed by a famous architect.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Past simple passive uses 'was' plus the past participle 'designed'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fill in the blank with the correct preposition (in, for, or as):
practicumQuestions.promptText: My brother works _____ an international tech firm in Jakarta.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the preposition that indicates the company a person works for.
practicumQuestions.explanation: We use 'work for' when specifying the company or organization.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the capitalization and punctuation errors in the sentence below:
practicumQuestions.promptText: the new manager started working at microsoft on monday.
practicumQuestions.hint: Check the beginning of the sentence, the company name, and the day of the week.
targetAnswers: The new manager started working at Microsoft on Monday.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Proper nouns such as 'Microsoft' and days like 'Monday' must be capitalized, along with the first word of the sentence.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Rewrite the sentence using the correct uncountable form of 'work':
practicumQuestions.promptText: I have three important works to finish before leaving.
practicumQuestions.hint: 'Work' is uncountable. Use 'a lot of work' or 'three tasks / jobs'.
targetAnswers: I have a lot of important work to finish before leaving.
I have three important jobs to finish before leaving.
I have three important tasks to finish before leaving.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The noun 'work' cannot take a plural 's'. Use 'jobs' or 'tasks' with numbers, or keep 'work' uncountable.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change the following active sentence into the Present Continuous Passive:
practicumQuestions.promptText: Technicians are repairing the computers right now.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'are being' plus the past participle 'repaired'.
targetAnswers: The computers are being repaired right now.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Present continuous passive uses 'is/are being' + past participle.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fill in the blank with the correct preposition (in, for, or as):
practicumQuestions.promptText: Sarah works _____ journalism and writes articles for major newspapers.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the preposition that refers to an industry or field.
practicumQuestions.explanation: We use 'work in' when talking about a professional field or industry like journalism.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the grammar and mechanics in the following sentence:
practicumQuestions.promptText: many products is exported to other countries every year.
practicumQuestions.hint: Check subject-verb agreement for plural nouns in the passive voice.
targetAnswers: Many products are exported to other countries every year.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The subject 'products' is plural, so it requires 'are' instead of 'is'.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Fill in the blank with the correct preposition (in, for, or as):
practicumQuestions.promptText: He started his career working _____ a professional chef in Paris.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the preposition that indicates a specific job title or profession.
practicumQuestions.explanation: We use 'work as' followed by a specific job title or profession.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write a complete sentence in the Present Perfect Passive using the prompts provided:
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'has been signed already' or 'has already been signed'.
targetAnswers: The contract has already been signed.
The contract has been signed already.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Present perfect passive is formed with 'has/have been' + past participle (signed).

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: What a Job!: Second Conditional & Work Vocabulary

content.summary: This speaking lab focuses on talking about hypothetical job scenarios using the Second Conditional, alongside professional work vocabulary. Clear word stress helps listeners follow your arguments when you discuss career choices, salaries, and working conditions.
content.audioGuidance: Pay close attention to sentence stress when forming hypothetical sentences. Emphasize the modal verb 'would' and the past form of the verb to show condition and result clearly. Keep your voice steady and pause slightly between clauses.

pillars.name: Second Conditional Rhythm
pillars.target: Balanced stress on 'if' clauses and modal results
pillars.explanation: When speaking about unreal situations, stress the key action verbs and the modal verb would to indicate imagination rather than reality.

pillars.name: Work Vocabulary Articulation
pillars.target: Crisp consonant clusters in professional terms
pillars.explanation: Pronounce multi-syllable terms like challenging, successful, and obsolete with correct primary stress on the correct syllable.

pillars.name: Intonation in Workplace Discussions
pillars.target: Falling intonation for statements and rising for conditional hypotheses
pillars.explanation: Use a rising tone in the condition clause and a falling tone in the result clause to sound natural and persuasive during professional discussions.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: Notice how multi-syllable adjectives shift their stress pattern depending on the root word and suffix.
Observe the stress placement on the first syllable of obsolete versus the second syllable of promoted.
Both are single syllable words with strong vowel sounds, requiring clear articulation in professional sentences.
Both nouns feature primary stress on the first syllable followed by a weak second syllable.

drills.targetText: If I had a better job, I would earn more money.
drills.phonetic: /ɪf aɪ hæd ə ˈbetə dʒɒb, aɪ wʊd ɜːn mɔː ˈmʌni/
drills.focus: Second conditional rhythm and weak form of would
drills.hint: Pronounce 'would' as /wəd/ and link 'had a' smoothly.

drills.targetText: She gave in her notice after getting promoted to store manager.
drills.phonetic: /ʃi ˈgeɪv ɪn hɜː ˈnəʊtɪs ˈɑːftə ˈgetɪŋ prəˈməʊtɪd tuː stɔːr ˈmænɪdʒə/
drills.focus: Phrasal verb 'give in' and work vocabulary linkage
drills.hint: Link the verb 'gave' with 'in' and stress the first syllable of notice.

drills.targetText: Many traditional jobs became obsolete because of new technology.
drills.phonetic: /ˈmeni trəˈdɪʃənl dʒɒbz bɪˈkeɪm ˈɒbsəliːt bɪˈkɒz ɒv nuː tekˈnɒlədʒi/
drills.hint: Ensure the first syllable of obsolete is prominent and clear.

drills.targetText: If the work was more challenging, employees would need better on-the-job training.
drills.phonetic: /ɪf ðə wɜːk wɒz mɔː ˈtʃælɪndʒɪŋ, ɪmˈplɔɪiːz wʊd niːd ˈbetə ɒn ðə dʒɒb ˈtreɪnɪŋ/
drills.focus: Complex second conditional structure and professional terms
drills.hint: Pause slightly after the comma before starting the main clause.

practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: Your manager asks why you deserve a promotion to store manager after completing your training.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: If I become store manager, I will ensure our team gets better on-the-job training.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪf aɪ bɪˈkʌm stɔːr ˈmænɪdʒə, aɪ wɪl ɪnˈʃʊə ˈaʊə tiːm gets ˈbetə ɒn ðə dʒɒb ˈtreɪnɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Maintain a professional tone and respond appropriately in a workplace dialogue.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Roleplay a conversation where you explain why you need to give in your notice.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are speaking with your supervisor to resign from your current job because you found a more successful company.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I am sorry to say this, but I need to give in my notice by the end of the week.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ æm ˈsɒri tuː seɪ ðɪs, bʌt aɪ niːd tuː gɪv ɪn maɪ ˈnəʊtɪs baɪ ði end ɒv ðə wiːk/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Express polite resignation phrasing with clear intonation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Roleplay discussing job benefits with a hiring manager during an interview.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: The interviewer asks what benefits matter most to you in a new job.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: For me, having paid holidays and good on-the-job training are extremely important.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /fɔː miː, ˈhævɪŋ peɪd ˈhɒlɪdeɪz ænd gʊd ɒn ðə dʒɒb ˈtreɪnɪŋ ɑːr ɪkˈstriːmli ɪmˈpɔːtənt/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Articulate job benefits naturally and fluently in an interview context.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Roleplay discussing obsolete jobs with a historian or colleague.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: Your colleague asks which traditional jobs no longer exist today.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Many jobs became obsolete because machines replaced human workers in factories.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈmeni dʒɒbz bɪˈkeɪm ˈɒbsəliːt bɪˈkɒz məˈʃiːnz rɪˈpleɪst ˈhjuːmən ˈwɜːkəz ɪn ˈfæktəriz/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Discuss historical workplace changes using correct vocabulary and descriptive verbs.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Produce a sentence incorporating the word 'successful' and the second conditional.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: If our business is successful next year, we will hire more staff.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪf ˈaʊə ˈbɪznɪs ɪz səkˈses.fəl nekst jɪə, wiː wɪl ˈhaɪə mɔː stɑːf/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Demonstrate precise use of the target vocabulary item in a grammatically correct sentence.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Produce a sentence using the Second Conditional structure to talk about an unreal work situation.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: If I didn't work every weekend, I would spend more time with my family.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪf aɪ ˈdɪdnt wɜːk ˈevri ˈwiːkend, aɪ wʊd spend mɔː taɪm wɪð maɪ ˈfæmɪli/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Check that the past simple appears in the if clause and would plus base verb in the main clause.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Read aloud the word 'challenging' and use it in a complete sentence with correct primary stress.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Finding a new job in a foreign country can be very challenging.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈfaɪndɪŋ ə nuː dʒɒb ɪn ə ˈfɒrɪn ˈkʌntri kæn biː ˈveri ˈtʃælɪndʒɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Emphasize the first syllable of 'challenging' clearly while keeping other syllables light.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Read this conditional sentence with a rising intonation on the condition clause and falling intonation on the result clause.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: If you worked harder, you might get promoted.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ɪf juː wɜːkt ˈhɑːdə, juː maɪt get prəˈməʊtɪd/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Ensure your voice rises slightly at the comma and falls clearly at the end of the sentence.
